title: Tic-Tac-Toe
summary: A minimal-looking game whose real interview test is generalizing the board and win condition — K-in-a-row on N x N — instead of hardcoding 3x3.

slides.markdown:
Tic-tac-toe looks trivial, which is the trap: the interview isn't testing whether you can hardcode a 3x3 grid, it's testing whether you can generalize the **board** and the **win rule** so the design survives a bigger board without a rewrite.

Spend your first two minutes locking three things out loud: board size, win condition (K-in-a-row), and players. UI, persistence, and matchmaking are out of scope unless asked.

The reframe that unlocks everything else: think of the board as a set of **lines** (rows, columns, diagonals), not a grid of independent cells.

Lock scope before designing anything. **In scope:** an N x N board (default 3x3), K-in-a-row win condition (default K=N), exactly two players taking alternating turns, draw detection when the board fills with no winner.

**Explicitly out of scope** unless the interviewer asks: AI difficulty tuning ("make the bot easy/medium/hard"), networked multiplayer with reconnect handling, and persistence across sessions. Naming these out loud signals you know the difference between the core design and its extensions — which is exactly what the later "extending to..." questions test.

Generalizing N and K up front is what turns a 15-minute toy problem into a 30-minute design conversation.

Six entities, each with one job. **Board** owns the grid and cell state — it does not know how to win. **Cell** is a single position, empty or holding a Symbol. **Symbol** is the enum (X, O). **Player** wraps a Symbol plus a move-selection strategy. **Game** owns turn order and orchestrates a round. **WinChecker** owns all win-detection logic.

The one decision worth defending out loud: why doesn't `Board` just check for a winner itself? Because win-checking is a *policy* (K-in-a-row, or later a totally different rule for Connect-Four) layered on top of board *state*. Separating them means you can swap the win rule without touching how the board stores moves.

The arrows that matter: `Game` depends on both `Board` and `WinChecker`, but `Board` has no dependency on `WinChecker` at all — the board never knows a game can be won. That one missing arrow is the whole design.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: checking a winner without rescanning the board
The hard part: winning lines are data, not code
slides.markdown:
The naive design writes four separate loops — one for rows, one for columns, one for each diagonal — and checks all four on every move. That's a maintenance trap: a Connect-Four variant or a 3D board needs its own hand-written loop set.

The fix: generate **every winning line once**, at construction, as a list of cell-coordinate lists. A row is one line, a column is one line, each diagonal is one line. Win-checking then becomes "does any line through the last move have every cell filled with the same symbol" — one piece of logic, reused for any board shape.

This is the single idea that makes the rest of the topic's extensions (Connect-Four, 3D, bigger K) nearly free.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: generating the line set once
Design patterns: Strategy for players, no State for turns
slides.markdown:
| Decision | Pattern | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Player move selection | **[Strategy](strategy-pattern)** — `PlayerStrategy` interface with `HumanStrategy`, `RandomBotStrategy`, `MinimaxStrategy` implementations | `Player` and `Game` don't care how a move is chosen; swapping strategies needs zero changes elsewhere |
| Whose turn it is | **No pattern** — one boolean or index flip after each move | Turn order here is a single alternation with no guarded transitions, no entry/exit actions — a full State machine is machinery solving a problem this doesn't have |

**How to decide:** reach for State only when a mode change triggers *behavior* differences elsewhere (see Chess's check/checkmate flow); a bare toggle doesn't earn the pattern.

A `RandomBotStrategy` just picks a uniformly random empty cell — good enough to demo the Strategy seam without extra complexity. A `MinimaxStrategy` explores the game tree: for each candidate move, recurse assuming the opponent plays optimally, and pick the move that maximizes your worst-case outcome. Alpha-beta pruning cuts branches that can't change the result, keeping it fast.

Minimax is fully tractable here because tic-tac-toe's game tree has at most 9! ≈ 362,880 states — trivial to search exhaustively even without pruning. Contrast that with [chess-game](chess-game): a mid-game position has roughly 35 legal moves and the tree explodes past what exhaustive search can touch, which is why real engines need evaluation functions and heavy pruning instead of solving to the end.

slides.sectionTitle: Deep-dive: Connect-Four as a reuse test
slides.markdown:
Connect-Four changes the win condition to "K-in-a-row anywhere on a taller board" and adds **gravity** — a move doesn't pick a cell, it picks a column, and the piece drops to the lowest empty row in it.

The reuse test: `WinChecker`'s line-set-plus-lookup design carries over completely unchanged, because a winning line is still just a list of coordinates checked for one matching symbol. The only new code is in `Board.placeMove(column)` — computing which row a dropped piece lands in — and in `generateLines`, which now needs K-length windows instead of full-board lines.

If your `WinChecker` needed a rewrite for this, that's a signal the original design leaked board-shape assumptions into the win-check logic.

A 4x4x4 board has far more winning lines than a 2D board: every row, column, and diagonal *within* each of the 4x4 layers, plus every line that cuts diagonally *through* layers (including the four "space diagonals" corner-to-corner). The count grows combinatorially with dimension, not linearly.

This is exactly why generating the line set **once, at construction** — not recomputing candidates per move — is what keeps `checkWinner` cheap: the expensive combinatorial work happens a single time, and every move afterward is just a lookup into `linesThrough(cell)` followed by a check over a handful of lines. Generating lines per-move would make every dimension bump a performance cliff instead of a one-time cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Concurrency: the real question is turn ordering, not locking
slides.markdown:
Tic-tac-toe is turn-based and single-writer by construction — one player moves at a time, so there's no shared-memory race to design around locally. Don't over-engineer a lock here; it's a tell that you've missed the actual scope.

The concurrency question interviewers actually ask is networked: two clients submit a move for the *same* turn at nearly the same time (a stale client resending, or a double-tap). The fix isn't locking the board — it's a **server-side turn-sequence check**: each move request carries the turn number it expects to act on, and the server rejects any move whose expected turn number doesn't match the current one. The first valid move wins; the second is rejected as stale.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: win-check logic duplicated per direction
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll just write a loop for rows, one for columns, one for each diagonal — four checks, done."

**Why it's wrong:** four hand-written loops means four places to get an off-by-one wrong, four places to update if K changes, and a rewrite for every new board shape (Connect-Four, 3D). It also usually re-scans the *entire* board on every move instead of just the lines through the last move, which is needless work at any board size.

**Correct model:** generate the full line set once as data (§6), and make win-checking one generic operation — "does any line through this cell match" — that never changes when the board's shape does.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: not validating a move before applying it
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The UI only lets you click empty cells, so the backend doesn't need to check."

**Why it's wrong:** any client-side assumption is a server-side vulnerability the moment there's an API between them — a replayed request, a race between two taps, or a malicious client can submit a move for the wrong turn or an already-filled cell. Silently accepting it corrupts board state: a cell now holds two players' claims, or the game accepted a ninth move when it should have ended at eight.

**Correct model:** `Game.playTurn(move)` validates two things before touching the board — it's this player's turn, and the target cell is empty — and rejects the move otherwise, before any state changes.
